iut_type: Generic/unspecified third-party USB Bluetooth dongle combined with a host product (projector) -- registration approach differs from a dedicated/bundled-accessory precedent
customer_question: We're developing a projector that uses a generic, commercially-available Bluetooth USB dongle (purchased separately by the end user, not a specific bundled accessory) to add Bluetooth PAN connectivity with a tablet for remote control. Is Bluetooth certification required for this kind of combination, and how would it be registered?
question_variants: Can a generic/unspecified third-party dongle be combined with the host product into one End Product registration, the way a dedicated accessory could?
If the dongle isn't part of the registration, what exactly needs to be registered?
actual_issue: The customer assumed that, similar to a known precedent (a home inkjet printer with an optional dedicated USB dongle enabling Bluetooth), their projector-plus-generic-dongle combination might either not require certification at all, or could be registered the same combined way -- but their dongle was an unspecified, generic commodity product rather than a dedicated bundled accessory.
plain_english_explanation: In the cited precedent, a home inkjet printer could be Bluetooth-enabled by the end user purchasing and attaching an optional USB dongle -- but because that dongle was a SPECIFIC, dedicated accessory tied to that exact printer model (with the printer itself holding Host Stack + Profile + application logic, and the dongle holding the Controller layer), the combination was registered together as one End Product (printer + dongle). For the projector case, however, the planned USB dongle is an unspecified, generic commodity product (the customer cited a specific commercial dongle model only as an example of the category, not as a fixed, dedicated accessory) -- so the same combined End Product registration approach is not available. This does NOT mean certification is unnecessary, though: instead, the projector itself (the host product) must be registered on its own as a Core-Host (the current term for what was previously called Host Subsystem), independent of whatever generic dongle a given end user happens to plug in.
consultant_answer: Since your dongle will be an unspecified, generic commercial product rather than a dedicated bundled accessory, you can't register it combined with the projector as one End Product the way the printer-plus-dongle precedent did. That doesn't mean certification isn't needed, though -- your projector itself needs to be registered on its own as a Core-Host (Host Subsystem), independent of whatever generic dongle an end user happens to attach.
decision_logic: When a host product relies on a Bluetooth USB dongle for connectivity, check whether the dongle is a specific, dedicated accessory tied to that exact product (enabling combined End Product registration covering both) or an unspecified, generic commodity product the end user sources independently (requiring the host product to be registered on its own as a Core-Host/Host Subsystem, since the variable dongle cannot be part of a fixed registration).
final_recommendation: When a customer describes a host-product-plus-dongle Bluetooth configuration, immediately ask whether the dongle is a specific dedicated accessory or a generic, end-user-sourced commodity product, since this distinction determines whether combined End Product registration is available or whether the host product must be registered independently as a Core-Host.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming a generic, swappable dongle can be folded into a combined End Product registration the way a dedicated accessory could would result in an invalid or incomplete registration that doesn't actually reflect the product's real configuration.
